en: Thus have I heard— *Dīgha Nikāya 16, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, desiring to attack the Vajjis,
spoke thus:
“I shall utterly destroy these Vajjis, so powerful and so majestic; I shall bring them to ruin; I shall lead them to disaster and calamity.
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha addressed the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha:

“Come, brahmin, go to the Blessed One; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and inquire after his health, asking: ‘Are you free from illness? Are you free from affliction? Are you light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort?’”

“Venerable sir, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha pays homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head; he inquires after your health, freedom from affliction, lightness of body, strength, and well-being.
And say this as well:
‘Venerable sir, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha desires to attack the Vajjis.’”
Therefore he spoke thus:
"I shall utterly destroy these Vajjis, who possess such great power and such great majesty; I shall bring them to ruin; I shall lead them to calamity and disaster.
Having thoroughly mastered what the Blessed One explains to you, please report it to me.
"For Tathāgatas do not speak what is false.
"So be it, sir," replied the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, to King Ajātasattu of Magadha.
Having assented to Vedehiputta, he had fine carriages harnessed, mounted each fine carriage, and set out from Rājagaha with those fine carriages. He proceeded toward Mount Gijjhakūṭa.

Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a carriage, he alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One on foot. Upon approaching, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged courteous and memorable greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha pays homage with his head at Master Gotama’s feet; he inquires after your health, freedom from illness, physical vigor, strength, and well-being.
Master Gotama, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha desires to attack the Vajjis."
Thus he spoke:
“I shall uproot these Vajjis, I shall destroy the Vajjis, I shall bring them to ruin and disaster.
2. The Factors of Non-Decline for a King
Now at that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, have you heard this: ‘The Vajjis hold frequent assemblies and are devoted to frequent gatherings’?”
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis frequently assemble and are frequent in their assemblies.
“As long as, Ānanda, the Vajjis frequently assemble and are frequent in their assemblies, growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘Do the Vajjis assemble in harmony, rise in harmony, and perform the affairs of the Vajjis in harmony?’”
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis assemble in harmony, they rise from their meetings in harmony, and they carry out the affairs of the Vajjis in harmony.
“As long as, Ānanda, the Vajjis assemble in harmony, rise from their meetings in harmony, and carry out the affairs of the Vajjis in harmony, growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.”

“Ānanda, have you heard this: ‘The Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, nor do they abolish what has been enacted; they proceed by undertaking and following the ancient Vajji traditions as they were originally laid down’?

“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, nor do they abolish what has been enacted; they proceed by undertaking and following the ancient Vajji traditions as they were originally laid down.
“As long, Ānanda, as the Vajjis do not enact what has not been enacted, nor do they abolish what has been enacted...”
“If they undertake and practice the ancient Vajjian traditions as they have been prescribed, Ānanda, growth alone is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘Do the Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and do they consider it right to listen to them?’”
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and they consider it right to listen to them.

“As long as, Ānanda, the Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and venerate those who are the elders among the Vajjis, and as long as they consider it right to listen to them, for that long, Ānanda, there will surely be growth.”
“The Vajjis may be expected to prosper, Ānanda, not to decline.
What have you heard, Ānanda, regarding this: ‘Do the Vajjis not dwell by means of forceful abduction of women from good families and girls from good families?
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis do not dwell by means of forceful abduction of women from good families and girls from good families.’”

“Ānanda, as long as the Vajjis do not allow women of good family and young girls of good family to live with them by force or by abduction, only growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
What have you heard, Ānanda: ‘The Vajjis honor, revere, esteem, and worship those shrines of the Vajjis, both internal and external, and they maintain what was formerly given and done to them’?”
“Do they not fail to provide us with our lawful tribute?
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis honor, respect, revere, and worship those shrines of the Vajjis, whether internal or external;
and they maintain what was formerly given and what was formerly performed for them.’”
“...and do not neglect our lawful tribute.
“As long, Ānanda, as the Vajjis honor, revere, esteem, and worship those Vajjian shrines— both those within and those without— and continue to offer what was formerly given to them...”
“They will not neglect the righteous tribute that has been performed in the past; only growth, Ānanda, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.

What have you heard, Ānanda, regarding this: ‘Is the righteous protection, defense, and security provided by the Vajjis for the arahants well-arranged, so that arahants who have not yet come might come to their realm, and those who have already come might dwell in comfort within their realm?’”

“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘The Vajjis provide righteous protection, defense, and security for the arahants—well-arranged so that arahants who have not yet come may come to their realm, and those who have already come may dwell at ease within their realm.

“As long as, Ānanda, the Vajjis provide righteous protection, defense, and security for the arahants—well-arranged so that arahants who have not yet come may come to their realm, and those who have already come may dwell at ease within their realm...”
“May they dwell in comfort. Ānanda, only growth is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline.
Then the Blessed One addressed Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha:
“Brahmin, on one occasion I was staying at Vesālī at the Sārandada Shrine.”
"There, Brahmin, I taught these seven principles of non-decline to the Vajjis.
As long as these seven principles of non-decline endure among the Vajjis,
and as long as the Vajjis are seen to conform to these seven principles of non-decline, growth alone, Brahmin, is to be expected for the Vajjis, not decline."
When this was said, the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Gotama, if the Vajjis were possessed of even a single quality that prevents decline, their growth alone could be expected, not their decline;
how much more so when they possess all seven qualities that prevent decline!"
“Indeed, Master Gotama, the Vajjis are not to be attacked by King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha in battle, except perhaps by means of bribery or by sowing dissension.
Come now, Master Gotama, we must go; we have many duties and much to do.
“Then, brahmin, go at your own convenience.”
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and departed.

Not long after Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, had left, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: 3. The Factors of Non-Decline for the Saṅgha of Monks Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: [as follows].
“Go, Ānanda, and assemble all the bhikkhus who dwell in dependence on Rājagaha in the assembly hall.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Having assembled all the bhikkhus who dwell in dependence on Rājagaha in the assembly hall, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"The Saṅgha of bhikkhus has assembled, venerable sir; now, venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems fit."
Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Sitting there, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, I will teach you seven principles that prevent decline."
“Listen to that and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, as long as the bhikkhus frequently assemble and are habitually frequent in assemblies, only growth, bhikkhus, is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.

And as long as the bhikkhus assemble in harmony, rise from their meetings in harmony, and carry out the business of the Saṅgha in harmony, only growth, bhikkhus, is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.”
"As long, monks, as the monks do not lay down what has not been laid down, do not abolish what has been laid down,
and practice by undertaking the training rules exactly as they have been laid down, growth alone is to be expected for the monks,
not decline."
"As long as, monks, the monks honor, revere, esteem, and worship those elder monks who have long been ordained, who are fathers to the Saṅgha and leaders of the Saṅgha,
and as long as they consider it their duty to listen to them, only growth, monks, is to be expected for the monks, not decline."
“Monks, as long as monks do not come under the power of arisen craving that leads to renewed existence, growth alone, monks, is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
As long as monks remain intent upon forest lodgings, growth alone, monks, is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
As long as monks establish mindfulness within themselves: ‘How might those who have not yet arrived…’”
"And may well-behaved fellow-practitioners come, and having come, may those well-behaved fellow-practitioners dwell in comfort.
Monks, as long as these seven factors conducive to non-decline remain among the monks, only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline. And as long as these...
“Bhikkhus, when bhikkhus are seen to conform to the seven qualities that prevent decline, only growth is to be expected for them, not decline.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, I will teach you seven other qualities that prevent decline; listen to that and attend closely, and I will speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Bhikkhus, as long as the bhikkhus do not delight in worldly activity, do not take pleasure in worldly activity, and are not devoted to delighting in worldly activity, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.”
"As long as, monks, the bhikkhus do not delight in talk, do not take pleasure in talk, and are not devoted to delighting in talk, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
And as long as, monks, the bhikkhus do not delight in sleep, do not take pleasure in sleep, and are not devoted to delighting in sleep, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline."
"As long as, monks, the monks do not delight in company, do not take pleasure in company, and are not devoted to the enjoyment of company, only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
As long as, monks, the monks do not have evil desires and do not fall under the sway of evil desires, only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline."
"As long, monks, as the bhikkhus do not have evil friends, evil companions, or evil associates, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
As long, monks, as the bhikkhus do not reach a premature conclusion because of a mere minor attainment of distinction, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
And as long, monks, as these seven factors of non-decline persist among the bhikkhus, and..."
If monks are seen to conform to these seven qualities that prevent decline, bhikkhus, only growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, I will teach you seven other qualities that prevent decline… [as before]….”
"And for as long, monks, as the bhikkhus shall be possessed of faith … [as above] … possessed of moral shame … possessed of moral dread …"
They will be learned;
they will be energetic;
they will be established in mindfulness.
They will be possessed of wisdom; monks, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.

As long as these seven factors conducive to non-decline endure among the bhikkhus, and as long as the bhikkhus are seen to conform to these seven factors conducive to non-decline, monks, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus.
“...it is to be expected, not decline.
Furthermore, monks, I will teach you seven other qualities that prevent decline; listen to them and pay close attention, and I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“As long, bhikkhus, as bhikkhus develop the enlightenment factor of mindfulness … [and] develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena …”
They will cultivate the enlightenment factor of energy;
they will cultivate the enlightenment factor of rapture;
they will cultivate the enlightenment factor of tranquility.
They will develop the enlightenment factor of concentration… they will develop the enlightenment factor of equanimity;
for as long, bhikkhus, as these seven factors of non-decline persist among the bhikkhus, and while these [conditions] exist, growth alone is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
As long, bhikkhus, as these seven factors of non-decline remain established among the bhikkhus...
“Bhikkhus, when bhikkhus are seen to conform to the seven qualities that prevent decline, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, I will teach you another seven qualities that prevent decline; listen to them and attend closely, and I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, for as long as bhikkhus develop the perception of impermanence … [as above] …”
They will cultivate the perception of non-self… they will cultivate the perception of foulness… they will cultivate the perception of danger…
If they will cultivate the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion,
and the perception of cessation, then, monks, growth is to be expected for these bhikkhus, not decline.
"Monks, as long as these seven principles that prevent decline remain established among the monks,
and as long as the monks are seen to conform to these seven principles that prevent decline, growth alone, monks,
is to be expected for the monks, not decline."
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the seven principles of non-decline. Listen to them and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, as long as monks maintain acts of loving-kindness through body toward their fellow practitioners, both openly and in private, growth alone is to be expected for these monks, not decline.
As long as monks maintain acts of loving-kindness through speech toward their fellow practitioners,

both openly and in private… [as above] …and as long as monks maintain acts of loving-kindness through mind toward their fellow practitioners, both openly and in private, growth alone is to be expected for these monks, not decline.”

"Monks, as long as monks share in common with their virtuous companions in the holy life those gains that are righteous and righteously obtained— even if it be only the mere contents of their alms-bowls— and do not consume such gains exclusively for themselves,
then, monks, growth is to be expected for the monks, not decline."

"And for as long, bhikkhus, as the bhikkhus dwell in commonality of virtue with their fellow brahmacārins— both openly and in private— in such virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration, for that long, bhikkhus, there will surely be growth."
This is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not their decline. For as long as, bhikkhus,

the bhikkhus dwell having attained a commonality of view with their fellow practitioners of the holy life regarding that view which is noble, leading out, and leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering— so long may they be expected to flourish, not to decline.
Whether in public or in private, monks, only growth is to be expected for the bhikkhus, not decline.
As long as these six factors conducive to non-decline endure among the bhikkhus,
and as long as the bhikkhus are seen to conform to these six factors conducive to non-decline, only growth, monks, is to be expected for the bhikkhus.
“...is to be expected, not decline.
While staying there at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, the Blessed One frequently gave this Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus:
“Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom.”
Concentration cultivated by virtue is of great fruit and great benefit.
Wisdom cultivated by concentration is of great fruit and great benefit.
The mind cultivated by wisdom is rightly liberated from the taints, namely:
“the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha for as long as he pleased, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Ambalaṭṭhikā.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, arrived at Ambalaṭṭhikā.
There the Blessed One stayed at Ambalaṭṭhikā in the Royal Resting Place.
While staying there at Ambalaṭṭhikā in the Royal Lodge, the Blessed One frequently gave this Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus:
"Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom.
Concentration fully developed by virtue is of great fruit and great benefit."
"Wisdom cultivated by concentration yields great fruit and brings great benefit.
The mind cultivated by wisdom is rightly liberated from the taints, namely:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance."
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Ambalaṭṭhikā for as long as he pleased, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Nāḷandā.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a great community of monks, arrived at Nāḷandā.
There, the Blessed One stayed near Nāḷandā in the Pāvārika mango grove.
4. Sāriputta’s Lion’s Roar

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:

“I have such confidence in the Blessed One, Bhante, that neither in the past, nor in the future, nor at present is there to be found another ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One in regard to this supreme enlightenment.”
“Magnificent indeed is this bull-like speech uttered by you, Sāriputta! You have taken a definitive stand and let out a lion’s roar:

‘Venerable sir, I am so confident in the Blessed One that neither in the past, nor in the future, nor at present is there, nor will there ever be, nor does there exist now, any other ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One in regard to supreme enlightenment.’”
“Sāriputta, have you encompassed with your mind the minds of all those who were in the past Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, so as to know them thus:
‘Those Blessed Ones had such virtue; they had such Dhamma, such wisdom, such conduct, and such liberation’?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“But, Sāriputta, do you encompass with your mind the minds of all those who will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future time, such that you know:
‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such virtue; those Blessed Ones will be of such Dhamma, such wisdom, such conduct, and such liberation’?
“No, indeed, Bhante.”
“But, Sāriputta, have you now, by encompassing my mind with your own mind, come to know me as I am now—the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—thus:
‘The Blessed One is of such virtue, of such Dhamma, of such wisdom, of such conduct, and of such liberation’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Moreover, Sāriputta, you do not possess the knowledge of encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Then why, Sāriputta, have you uttered such a sublime and bull-like speech, taken up a definitive position, and let out this lion’s roar:

‘Venerable sir, I am thus confident in the Blessed One: there has been, there will be, and there is not now found another ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One in regard to this supreme enlightenment’?”
“Venerable sir, I do not possess the knowledge of encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past, future, and present;
nevertheless, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.
Venerable sir, it is just as if there were a king’s frontier city with strong foundations, strong ramparts and arches, and a single gate.”
There, his gatekeeper would be wise, competent, and intelligent—one who keeps out strangers and lets in those he knows.
As he walked along the patrol path surrounding that city, he would not see any joint in the wall nor any opening in the wall, not even one large enough for a cat to slip through.
He would think to himself:
‘Whatever gross beings enter or exit this city, all of them enter or exit through this very gate.
Even so, Bhante, I have understood the logical sequence of the Dhamma:
‘Bhante, those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, in the past—all those Blessed Ones...’
Having abandoned the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— and with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
they developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are and awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And those, Bhante, who will be in the future time, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones— all those Blessed Ones [will do likewise].
Having abandoned the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— and with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
they will, by developing the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are,

awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. So too, venerable sir, the Blessed One now, being an arahant and a perfectly enlightened Buddha, has abandoned the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind...
“Having weakened the power of wisdom, with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness and having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are,
one has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
While staying there at Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove, the Blessed One frequently gave this very Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus:
“Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom.
Concentration cultivated by virtue is of great fruit and great benefit.
Wisdom cultivated by concentration is of great fruit and great benefit.”
“The mind, when fully developed by wisdom, is rightly liberated from the taints, namely:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.
5. The Danger of Immorality
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Nāḷandā for as long as he pleased, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Pāṭaligāma.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a great community of monks, arrived at Pāṭaligāma.
The lay followers of Pāṭaligāma heard: "The Blessed One has indeed arrived at Pāṭaligāma.
Then the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma approached the Blessed One; having approached, they [paid homage to] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to our guest house.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One,
and keeping him to their right, went to the rest-house. Having arrived,
they spread the rest-house with all kinds of rugs, prepared seats, and set out water-jars.
Having lit oil lamps, they approached the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the lay followers from Pāṭaligāma said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the rest house has been spread with all kinds of coverings, seats have been prepared, a water jar has been set out, and an oil lamp has been lit.”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One do as he deems it the right time.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and together with the community of monks, approached the guest house.
Having arrived, he washed his feet, entered the guest house, and sat down.
He sat down leaning against the middle pillar facing east.
The community of monks, having washed their feet and entered the rest-house, sat down leaning against the western wall facing east, with the Blessed One before them.
The lay followers of Pāṭaligāma, having washed their feet and entered the rest-house, sat down leaning against the eastern wall facing west, with the Blessed One before them.
Then the Blessed One addressed the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma:
“Householders, there are these five dangers for one who is immoral due to the failure in virtue.
What are the five?”
In this case, householders, an immoral person who has failed in virtue suffers a great loss of wealth due to negligence.
This is the first danger for an immoral person who has failed in virtue.
Furthermore, householders, an evil reputation spreads concerning an immoral person who has failed in virtue.
This is the second danger for one who is immoral due to their failure in virtue.
Furthermore, householders, whenever an immoral person who has failed in virtue approaches any assembly—
whether an assembly of kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, or ascetics— he does so without confidence.
He approaches [others] feeling abashed.
This is the third disadvantage for an immoral person due to their failure in virtue.
Furthermore, householders, an immoral person who has failed in virtue dies confused.
This is the fourth danger for one who is immoral due to their failure in virtue.
Furthermore, householders, an immoral person who has failed in virtue, with the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even hell.
This is the fifth danger for one who is immoral due to their failure in virtue.
Householders, these are the five dangers for one who is immoral due to the failure of virtue.
6. Benefits of Virtue:
Householders, there are these five benefits for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Which five?
Here, householders, one who is virtuous and perfect in virtue acquires a great mass of wealth through diligence.
This is the first benefit for one who is virtuous, from the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, a good report of one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue spreads abroad.
This is the second benefit of being virtuous and endowed with virtue.
Furthermore, householders, whatever assembly a person who is virtuous and endowed with virtue approaches—whether it be...
Whether it be an assembly of kṣatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics,
he approaches with confidence and without timidity.
This is the third benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue dies unconfused.
This is the fourth benefit for the virtuous person through the perfection of virtue.
Furthermore, householders, one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“This is the fifth benefit for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
These, householders, are the five benefits for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma with a discourse on the Dhamma for much of the night, dismissed them.
“The night has passed, householders; it is now time for you to do as you see fit.
“Very well, Bhante,” the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma replied to the Blessed One. They rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, they departed.
Then, not long after the lay followers of Pāṭaligāma had left, the Blessed One entered an empty dwelling.
7. Entering the City of Pāṭaliputta.
Now at that time, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, were building a city at the village of Pāṭali as a bulwark against the Vajjis.
At that time, many thousands of deities were taking possession of sites in the village of Pāṭali.
In whatever place powerful deities take possession of sites, the minds of powerful kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences there.
In whatever place middling deities take possession of sites, the minds of middling kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences there.
In whatever place inferior deities take possession of sites, the minds of inferior kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences there.
With his purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, the Blessed One saw those deities who were taking possession of sites in Pāṭaligāma all at once.
Then, rising at the time of dawn during the night, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, who is building a city in Pāṭaligāma?”
“Venerable sir, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, are building a city at Pāṭaligāma to ward off the Vajjis. “Ānanda,
just as if they had consulted with the gods of the Thirty-three,
even so, Ānanda, do Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, build a city at Pāṭaligāma to ward off the Vajjis.”
"Here, Ānanda, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw many deities—indeed thousands of them—taking possession of sites in Pāṭaligāma.
In whatever place, Ānanda, deities of great power take possession of sites, there the minds of powerful kings and royal ministers incline toward building dwellings."
In whatever place middle-ranking deities take possession of sites, there the minds of middle-ranking kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences.
In whatever place low-ranking deities take possession of sites, there the minds of low-ranking kings and royal ministers incline toward building residences.
To the extent, Ānanda, that there is a noble domain, to the extent that there is a marketplace—this city of Pāṭaliputta, a center of trade, shall be the foremost.
“Ānanda, there will be three obstacles to Pāṭaliputta:
either from fire, or from water, or from internal dissension.
Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they stood to one side. Standing there, Sunīdha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
"May the venerable Gotama accept today’s meal from us, together with the community of monks.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance,
went to their own residence. Having arrived, they had exquisite hard and soft food prepared in their residence and had the time announced to the Blessed One:
“Sir Gotama, it is time; the meal is ready.

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of Sunīdha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, together with the community of monks; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
He sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, with their own hands served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
When Sunidha and Vassakāra, the two chief ministers of Magadha, were seated to one side, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation with these verses:
“In whatever place a person of wise nature makes his dwelling, ...”
Having fed here those who are virtuous,
self-restrained, and living the holy life,
whatever deities were present there—
One should dedicate the offering to them;
when they are honored, they honor him in return, and when they are respected, they show respect to him.
Then the deities show him compassion,
just as a mother does for her own biological son;
a person who is thus favored by the deities—
“...one always sees auspicious things.
Then the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation to Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, with these verses, rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, Sunidha and Vassakāra, the chief ministers of Magadha, followed closely behind the Blessed One, thinking:
“By whichever gate the ascetic Gotama shall depart today, that shall be known as ‘Gotama’s Gate.
By whichever ford he shall cross the river Gaṅgā, that shall be known as ‘Gotama’s Ford.
Then, by whichever gate the Blessed One departed, that became known as ‘Gotama’s Gate.’
Then the Blessed One approached the river Gaṅgā.
Now at that time, the river Gaṅgā was full to the brim, so that a crow could drink from it.
Some people were searching for boats, some were searching for rafts, and some were binding together a raft, desiring to go from this shore to the further shore.
Then the Blessed One— just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from the near bank of the river Gaṅgā and reappeared on the far bank together with the community of monks.

The Blessed One saw those people, some of whom were searching for a boat, some of whom were searching for a raft, and some of whom were binding together a float, desiring to go from the hither shore to the further shore.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“Those who cross the ocean, the lake...”
Having built a bridge and left behind the marshes,
people indeed construct a raft;
but it is the wise who have already crossed over.
The First Recitation Section.
8. Discourse on the Noble Truths.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Koṭigāma.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a great community of monks, arrived at Koṭigāma.
There the Blessed One stayed at Koṭigāma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that we and you have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time.
Of which four?
Monks, it is through the non-awakening and non-penetration of the noble truth of suffering that we, as well as you, have wandered and transmigrated for such a long time.
Monks, it is through the non-awakening and non-penetration of the noble truth of the origin of suffering that we, as well as you, have wandered and transmigrated for such a long time.
“Monks, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating the noble truth of the cessation of suffering that we have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time—both I and you.
Monks, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering that we have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time—both I and you.
But now, monks, this noble truth of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; the noble truth of the origin of suffering... [has been awakened to and penetrated].”
The noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated.
Craving for existence has been cut off; the conduit to existence has been exhausted;
there is now no further becoming.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“Of the four noble truths, ...”
Through not seeing things as they truly are,
one has wandered for a long time through this or that very birth.
These views have been seen through,
the conduit to existence has been uprooted;
the root of suffering is cut off.
“There is now no further becoming.
While staying there at Koṭigāma, the Blessed One frequently gave this Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus:
“Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom.”
Concentration cultivated by virtue is of great fruit and great benefit.
Wisdom cultivated by concentration is of great fruit and great benefit.
The mind cultivated by wisdom is rightly liberated from the taints, namely:
“the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.

Then, having stayed at Koṭigāma for as long as he pleased, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: [9. Anāvattidhammasambodhiparāyaṇa] “... destined for enlightenment and no longer subject to falling back.”
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Nādika.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, arrived at Nādika.
There, at Nādikā, the Blessed One was staying in the Brick Hall.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, a bhikkhu named Sāḷha has passed away at Nādikā. What is his destination? What is his future state?"
"Venerable sir, the bhikkhunī named Nandā has died at Nātika; what is her destination, what is her future state?
Venerable sir, the lay follower named Sudatta has died at Nātika; what is his destination, what is his future state?
Venerable sir, the female lay follower named Sujātā has died at Nātika; what is her destination, what is her future state?"
"Venerable sir, the lay follower named Kukkuṭa has passed away at Nātika; what is his destination, what is his future state?
Venerable sir, the lay follower named Kāḷimbo has passed away...
Venerable sir, the lay follower named Nikaṭa has passed away..."
"Venerable sir, there was a lay follower named Kaṭissaha… a lay follower named Tuṭṭha… a lay follower named Santuṭṭha."
“Venerable sir, the lay follower named Bhadda...
the lay follower named Subhadda has died at Nātika; what is his destination, what is his future state?

“Ānanda, through the destruction of the taints, the bhikkhu Sāḷha, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, entered and dwelt therein.”
“Ānanda, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, the bhikkhunī Nandā is of spontaneous birth; she will attain final nibbāna there and is not subject to returning from that world.

Ānanda, through the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, the lay follower Sudatta is a once-returner who, having come back to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering.

Ānanda, through the complete destruction of three fetters, the female lay follower Sujātā is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and headed for full enlightenment.”
Ānanda, the lay follower Kukkuṭa, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there,
not subject to return from that world. Ānanda, the lay follower Kāḷimbo … [and] the lay follower Nikaṭa … [are likewise].
Kaṭissaha, Ānanda, was a lay follower … Tuṭṭha, Ānanda,
was a lay follower … Santuṭṭha, Ānanda, was a lay follower …

“Ānanda, the lay follower Bhadda… the lay follower Subhadda, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, has become one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.

Ānanda, more than fifty lay followers have passed away at Nātika; through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, they have become those of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.”

“Ānanda, more than ninety lay followers have passed away in Nātika; through the total destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, they are once-returners who, having come back to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering.

Ānanda, more than five hundred lay followers have passed away in Nātika; through the total destruction of the three fetters, they are stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.
10. The Discourse on the Gift of the Dhamma and the Way of the Dhamma.
"It is not surprising, Ānanda, that one who has become human should pass away.
That you should approach the Tathāgata and ask about this matter after he has passed away would be a source of vexation for the Tathāgata.

Therefore, Ānanda, I will teach you a discourse on the Dhamma called 'The Mirror of the Dhamma,' endowed with which a noble disciple, if he so desires, may declare of himself: [that he has attained final knowledge]."

“I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal womb; I have exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.
And what, Ānanda, is that mirror of the Dhamma, that exposition of the Dhamma, endowed with which a noble disciple, if he so desires, may himself declare of himself:

“I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal womb; I have exhausted the realm of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment”?
Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha, [thinking]:

"The Blessed One is indeed an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, a knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma...
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way...’
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the right way; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples consists of these four pairs of persons, these eight types of individuals.
This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’”
“He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
This, Ānanda, is that mirror of the Dhamma, that exposition of the Dhamma, endowed with which a noble disciple, if he so desires, may declare of himself:

‘I am one who has exhausted hell, exhausted the animal realm, exhausted the sphere of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower worlds. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.’”
While staying there at Nādikā in the Brick House, the Blessed One frequently gave this very discourse on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus:
"Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom.
Concentration, when fully developed by virtue, is of great fruit and great benefit."
"Wisdom cultivated by concentration yields great fruit and brings great benefit.
The mind cultivated by wisdom is rightly liberated from the taints, namely:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance."
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Nādika as long as he pleased, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Vesālī.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a great community of monks, arrived at Vesālī.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove.
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending;
this is our instruction to you.
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful?”
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … [as before] … he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind … [as before] …
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, monks, a monk is mindful.
And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending?
Here, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; and he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
He acts with clear comprehension; whether going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he acts with clear comprehension.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is clearly comprehending.
A monk, monks, should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending.
“This is our instruction to you.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan heard: “The Blessed One has arrived at Vesālī and is staying at Vesālī in my mango grove.”

Then the courtesan Ambapālī had her finest carriages harnessed, mounted each of her fine carriages, and set out from Vesālī with her fine carriages. She drove as far as the ground would allow for a carriage toward her own park;
having gone by carriage as far as it could go, she alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As Ambapālī the courtesan was sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One, together with the community of bhikkhus, accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to her right, departed.
The Licchavis of Vesālī heard: “It is said that the Blessed One has arrived at Vesālī and is staying at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove.”
Then those Licchavis had their various fine carriages yoked; mounting each of their fine carriages, they set out from Vesālī in their various fine carriages.
Among them, some Licchavis were blue—blue in complexion, dressed in blue garments, and adorned with blue ornaments;
some Licchavis were yellow—yellow in complexion, dressed in yellow garments, and adorned with yellow ornaments; some Licchavis were red—red in complexion...
Some Licchavis were red—red in complexion, wearing red garments, and adorned with red ornaments; others were white—white in complexion, wearing white garments, and adorned with white ornaments.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan drove axle against axle, wheel against wheel, and yoke against yoke with the young Licchavis.
Then those Licchavis said this to Ambapālī the courtesan:
“Hey, Ambapālī, why were you wheeling axle against axle, wheel against wheel, and yoke against yoke with the young Licchavis?
“Because, noble sirs, the Blessed One has been invited by me for tomorrow’s meal, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Give up this meal, Ambapālī, for a hundred thousand pieces of gold!”
“Even if you were to give me Vesālī together with its revenues, noble sirs, I still would not give you that meal.
Then those Licchavis snapped their fingers, saying:
“We have been defeated, alas! We have been defeated, alas! by Ambakā!”
Then those Licchavis set out for Ambapālī’s Grove.
The Blessed One saw those Licchavis coming from afar.
Having seen them, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, for those bhikkhus who have never before seen the Tāvatiṃsa gods, look at the Licchavi assembly, bhikkhus!
Behold the Licchavi assembly, bhikkhus!
Compare the Licchavi assembly, bhikkhus!”
"...just like those of the Thirty-three [gods].

Then those Licchavis, having gone by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a carriage, alighted from their carriages and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened those Licchavis with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then those Licchavis, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept tomorrow’s meal from us, together with the community of bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One said this to those Licchavis:
“Licchavis, I have already accepted Ambapālī the courtesan’s meal for tomorrow.
Then those Licchavis snapped their fingers, saying:
“Alas, we have been defeated by Ambakā! Alas, we have been defeated by Ambakā!”
Then those Licchavis, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to their right, departed.
Then, at the end of that night, the courtesan Ambapālī had various kinds of excellent hard and soft food prepared in her own park and had the time announced to the Blessed One:
"It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready."

Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of Ambapālī the courtesan together with the community of monks; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Ambapālī the courtesan, with her own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then the courtesan Ambapālī, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As she was sitting there, the courtesan Ambapālī said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I give this park to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha."
The Blessed One accepted the park.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Ambapālī the courtesan with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
While staying there at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s grove, the Blessed One frequently gave this very discourse on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus:
“Such is virtue, such is concentration, such is wisdom.
Concentration cultivated by virtue is of great fruit and great benefit.
Wisdom cultivated by concentration is of great fruit and great benefit.”
“The mind, when fully developed by wisdom, is rightly liberated from the taints, namely:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.
12. The Rainy-Season Retreat at Veḷuva Village.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed in Ambapālī’s grove for as long as he pleased, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to the village of Veḷuva.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with a great community of monks, arrived at the village of Veḷuva.
There the Blessed One stayed at Veḷuvagāmaka.
There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
“Come, monks, spend the rains retreat around Vesālī, each according to your friends, your acquaintances, and your associates.
But I shall spend the rains retreat right here in the village of Veḷuva.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One, and they spent the rains retreat around Vesālī, each according to their friends, acquaintances, and associates.
The Blessed One, however, entered the rains retreat right there in the village of Veḷuva.
Then, while the Blessed One had entered the rains retreat, a severe illness arose in him; agonizing, deathly pains assailed him.
Yet the Blessed One endured them mindfully and clearly comprehending, without being disturbed.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"It would not be fitting for me to attain final nibbāna without having addressed my attendants and without taking leave of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Suppose I were to suppress this illness with energy and dwell having resolved upon the life-faculty?"
Then the Blessed One, having overcome that affliction through energy and having resolved upon the life-force, remained there.
Then that affliction of the Blessed One subsided.
Then the Blessed One, having recovered from his illness and not long after his recovery, went out from his dwelling and sat down on a seat prepared in the shade of the dwelling.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“I have seen, Bhante, that the Blessed One is at ease; I have seen, Bhante, that the Blessed One is bearing up well. However, Bhante, my body feels as if it has become heavy, and the directions no longer appear clear to me.”
“Even the Dhamma does not occur to me because of the Blessed One’s illness. Yet, Bhante, I had some small measure of consolation:
‘The Blessed One will not pass away into final Nibbāna until he has said something concerning the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“But what, Ānanda, does the Saṅgha of bhikkhus expect of me?”
"Ānanda, I have taught the Dhamma without making any distinction between inner and outer;
Ānanda, there is no 'teacher's fist' regarding the Dhammas of the Tathāgata.
Now, Ānanda, suppose someone were to think thus:"
‘I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,’ or ‘The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is under my guidance’—surely, Ānanda, such a person would say something concerning the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
But it does not occur to the Tathāgata, Ānanda, in this way:
‘I shall lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,’ or ‘The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is under my guidance.’
"Once, Ānanda, the Tathāgata will say something concerning the community of monks.
But now, Ānanda, I am aged, old, advanced in years, having reached the end of my journey;
my age has reached eighty."
"Just as, Ānanda, an old cart is kept going by means of a patchwork of straps, even so, Ānanda,
it seems that the body of the Tathāgata is kept going by means of a patchwork of straps.
At whatever time, Ānanda, the Tathāgata— through non-attention to all signs and through the subsiding of certain feelings— "[attains the cessation of perception and feeling]."
Having attained and dwelling in the signless concentration of mind through cessation, Ānanda, at that time the body of the Tathāgata becomes more comfortable.
Therefore, Ānanda, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; dwell with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu dwell with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
[He dwells] in feelings …pe…

He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
“Ānanda, whoever now, or after my passing, shall dwell with themselves as an island,
with themselves as a refuge and no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge and no other refuge—
those monks, Ānanda, who desire training, will be foremost among my disciples.”
The Second Recitation Section.
13. Discourse on the Appearance of Signs.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Vesālī and returned from his almsround after the meal, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Take up your sitting mat, Ānanda;
we shall go to the Cāpāla Shrine for the day’s abiding.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Taking his sitting mat, he followed closely behind the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One went to the Cāpāla Shrine; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
The Venerable Ānanda, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:

“Ānanda, there are these eight causes, these eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
What are the eight?

Furthermore, Ānanda, suppose there is a recluse or a brahmin who possesses psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind, or a deva of great power and great majesty;
he has cultivated a limited perception of earth and an immeasurable perception of water.
He causes this earth to tremble, to shake, to quiver, and to quake.
This is the second cause, the second condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Tusita realm, descends into his mother’s womb mindful and clearly comprehending, then this earth shakes, trembles, and quakes violently.
This is the third cause, the third condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Bodhisatta emerges mindfully and clearly comprehending from his mother’s womb, then this earth shakes, trembles, and quakes violently.
This is the fourth cause, the fourth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.

This is the fifth cause, the fifth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and convulses.
This is the sixth cause, the sixth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquishes the life-formations, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and convulses.
This is the seventh cause, the seventh condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and convulses.
This is the eighth cause, the eighth condition for the manifestation of a great earthquake.
These, Ānanda, are the eight causes and eight conditions for the manifestation of a great earthquake.

18. The Eight Bases of Mastery.
“Ānanda, there are these eight bases of mastery.
What are the eight?
One percipient of forms internally sees forms externally, limited, beautiful or ugly.”
Having mastered them, he perceives thus: "I know, I see.
This is the first base of mastery.
One who is percipient of forms internally sees forms externally, immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.
Having mastered them, one perceives thus: "I know, I see.
This is the second sphere of mastery.
Internally perceiving no form, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the third base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.
Having mastered them, he is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.
This is the fourth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster.
Just as an umā flower is blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster;
or just as that cloth from Bārāṇasī, smooth on both sides, is blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster— even so,
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue-colored, blue in appearance, and blue in luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the fifth base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Just as a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance,
and yellow in luster; or just as Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster— even so,
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Having mastered them, he has the perception: ‘I know, I see.
This is the sixth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, red-colored, red in appearance, and red in luster;
or just as that cloth from Varanasi, smooth on both sides, is red, red-colored,
red in appearance, and red in luster.
In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red-colored, red-appearing, and red-luminous.
Having mastered them, one has the perception: "I know, I see.
This is the seventh base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Just as, for example, the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster;
or just as, for example, Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are white, of white color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Having mastered them, one has the perception: "I know, I see.
This is the eighth base of mastery.
"These, Ānanda, are the eight bases of mastery.
19. The Eight Liberations:
These, Ānanda, are the eight liberations."
Which eight?
Possessing form, one sees forms;
this is the first liberation.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally;
this is the second liberation.
One is intent only on the beautiful.
This is the third liberation.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space;
this is the fourth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite space, perceiving "consciousness is infinite," one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness;
this is the fifth liberation.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving "there is nothing," one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This is the sixth liberation.
Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the seventh liberation.
By completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling;
this is the eighth liberation.
These, Ānanda, are the eight liberations.

30. Persons Worthy of a Stupa:
Ānanda, there are these four persons worthy of a stupa.
Which four?

The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of a stupa; the Paccekabuddha is worthy of a stupa; the disciple of the Tathāgata is worthy of a stupa; and the Wheel-turning Monarch is worthy of a stupa.
And for what reason, Ānanda, is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, worthy of a stupa?
‘This is the stupa of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,’ Ānanda—thus many people will develop a serene mind.
Having developed a serene mind there, with the breakup of the body, after death, they will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
It is for this purpose, Ānanda, that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of a stupa.

It is for this reason, Ānanda, that a disciple of the Tathāgata is worthy of a stupa.
And for what reason, Ānanda, is a wheel-turning monarch worthy of a stupa?
‘This is the stupa of that righteous Dhamma-king,’ Ānanda, many people will thus develop confidence in their hearts.
Having developed confidence there, with the breakup of the body, after death, they will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
It is for this purpose, Ānanda, that a wheel-turning monarch is worthy of a stupa.
"These, Ānanda, are the four who are worthy of a stupa.
