“Too soon the Blessed One will attain final nibbāna; too soon the Sugata will attain final nibbāna; too soon the Eye of the World will vanish.

Then the Mallas, the sons of the Mallas, the daughters-in-law of the Mallas, and the wives of the Mallas—distressed, sorrowful, and overcome with mental anguish—approached the Upavattana sal grove of the Mallas where the Venerable Ānanda was staying.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:

“If I were to have each individual Mallian of Kosinārā pay homage to the Blessed One one by one, the Blessed One would not be finished being honored by the Mallians of Kosinārā before this night dawns.
What if I were to have the Mallians of Kosinārā arranged family by family and have them pay homage to the Blessed One, saying:
‘Venerable Sir, the Mallian named so-and-so, together with his children, his wife, his retinue, and his kinsmen, pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One with his head’?”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having arranged the Mallas of Kusinārā in groups of families, had them pay homage to the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable sir, the Malla named so-and-so, together with his children, his wife, his retinue, and his kinsmen, pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One with his head.
In this manner, during the very first watch of the night, the Venerable Ānanda had the Mallas of Kusinārā pay homage to the Blessed One.
34. The Story of the Wanderer Subhadda.
Now at that time, a wanderer named Subhadda was staying in Kusinārā.
The wanderer Subhadda heard:
“Today, it is said, in the last watch of the night, the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the ascetic Gotama will take place.
Then this occurred to the wanderer Subhadda:
“I have indeed heard from elder and aged wanderers, from teachers and preceptors, as they were speaking:”
“‘Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, arise in the world only once in a long, long time.
This very night, in the last watch, the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the ascetic Gotama will take place.
And this state of doubt has arisen within me.”
“I have such confidence in the ascetic Gotama that he is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might abandon this state of doubt.
Then the wanderer Subhadda went to the Mallas’ Sal Grove at Upavattana where the Venerable Ānanda was staying. Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“I have heard this, Master Ānanda, from elder wanderers, aged and advanced, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:”
“‘Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, arise in the world only once in a great while.
This very night, in the last watch, the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the ascetic Gotama will take place.
And this state of doubt has arisen in me:”
“Having such confidence in the ascetic Gotama, I think: ‘The ascetic Gotama is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might abandon this state of doubt.
It would be well, Master Ānanda, if I might obtain a sight of the ascetic Gotama.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the wanderer Subhadda:
“Enough, friend Subhadda; do not trouble the Tathāgata. The Blessed One is weary.
A second time, the wanderer Subhadda...
[and] a third time, the wanderer Subhadda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“I have heard this, Master Ānanda, from elder wanderers, those who are aged, advanced, and teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:
‘Only once in a long, long time do Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise in the world.
This very night, in the last watch, the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the ascetic Gotama will take place.”
"Moreover, this state of doubt has arisen in me:
'I have such confidence in the ascetic Gotama that he is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might abandon this state of doubt.
It would be well, Master Ānanda, if I could obtain a sight of the ascetic Gotama."
A third time, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the wanderer Subhadda:
“Enough, friend Subhadda; do not trouble the Tathāgata. The Blessed One is weary.
The Blessed One heard this conversation between the Venerable Ānanda and the wanderer Subhadda.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Enough, Ānanda; do not prevent Subhadda. Let Subhadda have the opportunity to see the Tathāgata.
Whatever Subhadda asks me, he will ask out of a desire for knowledge, not out of a desire to trouble me.”
"And whatever I answer when questioned by him, he will quickly understand it.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the wanderer Subhadda:
"Go, friend Subhadda; the Blessed One grants you an opportunity."
Then the wanderer Subhadda approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the wanderer Subhadda said this to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, as for those recluses and brahmins who have orders, followings, and are teachers of groups; who are well-known and famous founders of sects, esteemed as holy by many people— namely, Pūraṇa Kassapa,
Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta,
and Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta— did they all, according to their own claim, directly know [the truth], or did none of them directly know it, or did some directly know it while others did not?”
“Enough, Subhadda, let this be:
‘Did they all realize it for themselves according to their own claim, or did none of them realize it, or did some realize it and some not?
I will teach you the Dhamma, Subhadda.”
“Listen to this and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Subhadda the wanderer replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Subhadda, in whatever Dhamma and Discipline the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, there no ascetic is found;
there no second ascetic is found; there no third ascetic is found; there no fourth ascetic is found.”
But in whatever Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found, there a recluse is found;
there a second recluse is found; there a third recluse is found;
and there a fourth recluse is found.
"In this Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found;
here alone, Subhadda, is there a recluse, here a second recluse, here a third recluse, here a fourth recluse. The doctrines of others are empty of recluses.
And if these monks, Subhadda, were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants."
Twenty-nine years of age, Subhadda,
was I when I went forth seeking what is wholesome;
fifty-three years have passed since then.
Since I went forth, Subhadda,
I have been a follower of a portion of the true Dhamma;
outside of this, there is no ascetic at all.
There is no second ascetic;
there is no third ascetic;
there is no fourth ascetic.
“Empty are the doctrines of other sectarians of true recluses.
But if, Subhadda, these monks were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants.
When this was said, the wanderer Subhadda addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!

Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
"In this very way, the Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma by means of many methods.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, venerable sir; may I receive full ordination."
“Subhadda, whoever was formerly a member of another sect who desires the going-forth and desires the full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline must wait four months as a probationer.
At the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with his mind,
they grant him the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu.”
"Moreover, I understand the distinction between individuals in this matter.
"Venerable sir, if those who were formerly members of other sects, desiring the going-forth and desiring the full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline,
must wait four months in probation, then at the end of those four months, if the bhikkhus are satisfied with them— "
“They grant the going-forth and ordain them into the state of a bhikkhu. ‘I shall undergo the probation for four years;
at the end of those four years, may the bhikkhus, with minds inclined toward me, grant me the going-forth and ordain me into the state of a bhikkhu.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Therefore, Ānanda, let Subhadda go forth.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the wanderer Subhadda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“It is a gain for you, friend Ānanda;
it is well gained by you, friend Ānanda, that you have been consecrated here in the presence of the Teacher with the consecration of a resident pupil.
Then the wanderer Subhadda received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.
Not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Subhadda, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,

soon realized for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; having attained it, he dwelt therein.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Subhadda became one of the Arahants;
he was the last personal disciple of the Blessed One.
The Fifth Recitation Section.
35. The Last Words of the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Now, Ānanda, it may occur to you:
‘The teaching has lost its Teacher; we have no Teacher.
But, Ānanda, this should not be viewed in such a way.
"Ānanda, whatever Dhamma and Vinaya have been taught and laid down by me for you, that shall be your teacher after my passing away.
Furthermore, Ānanda, just as monks at present address one another with the term 'friend' (āvuso), they should not address one another in that way after my passing away.
An elder monk, Ānanda, should address a junior monk by his name, or by his clan, or by the term 'friend.'"
"A junior monk, Ānanda, should address a more senior monk as 'Venerable Sir' or 'Worthy One.
After my passing, Ānanda, the Saṅgha may, if it so desires, abolish the minor and lesser training rules.
After my passing, Ānanda, the Brahma-punishment should be imposed upon the monk Channa."
“But what, venerable sir, is the Brahma-punishment?
“Ānanda, whatever Channa the bhikkhu wishes, that he may say.
He is not to be addressed by the bhikkhus, nor exhorted, nor instructed.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"It may be, bhikkhus, that even a single bhikkhu has doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice. Ask, bhikkhus; do not later feel regret, saying:
'The Teacher was present before us, yet we were not able to question the Blessed One in his presence.'"
When this was said, those bhikkhus became silent.
A second time the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus...
A third time the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, it may be that even a single bhikkhu has some doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice. Ask, bhikkhus; do not later feel regret, saying:
‘The Teacher was present before us, yet we were not able to question the Blessed One in his presence.
For a third time, those bhikkhus remained silent.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“It may be, bhikkhus, that out of respect for the Teacher you do not ask. Let a friend, bhikkhus, inform his friend.
When this was said, those bhikkhus remained silent.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:

“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante! I have such confidence, Bhante, in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus that I do not see even a single bhikkhu who has any doubt or perplexity regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice.”
“You speak of faith, Ānanda, but it is actually knowledge that belongs to the Tathāgata in this matter.
There is not even a single bhikkhu in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who has doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice.
For among these five hundred bhikkhus, even the one who is the least is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.”
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Now, bhikkhus, I exhort you:
'All conditioned phenomena are subject to decay; strive with diligence.'"
"This is the Tathāgata’s last word.
36. Discourse on the Final Nibbāna:
Then the Blessed One entered the first jhāna; emerging from the first jhāna, he entered the second jhāna.
He entered [the first jhāna]; having emerged from the second jhāna, he entered the third jhāna;
having emerged from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna; having emerged from the fourth jhāna, he entered the base of infinite space;
having emerged from the attainment of the base of infinite space, he entered the base of infinite consciousness; having emerged from the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness...
Having emerged from that, he entered the base of nothingness; having emerged from the attainment of the base of nothingness, he entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
having emerged from the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the cessation of perception and feeling.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Venerable Anuruddha, the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna.
“Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has not attained final Nibbāna; he has entered the cessation of perception and feeling.
Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

He entered [the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception]; having emerged from the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the base of nothingness;
having emerged from the attainment of the base of nothingness, he entered the base of infinite consciousness;
having emerged from the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, he entered the base of infinite space; having emerged from the attainment of the base of infinite space...
He attained the fourth jhāna; emerging from the fourth jhāna, he attained the third jhāna;
emerging from the third jhāna, he attained the second jhāna; emerging from the second jhāna, he attained the first jhāna;
emerging from the first jhāna, he attained the second jhāna; emerging from the second jhāna...
Emerging from that, he attained the third jhāna; emerging from the third jhāna, he attained the fourth jhāna;
emerging from the fourth jhāna, immediately thereafter the Blessed One passed away into final Nibbāna.
When the Blessed One had passed away into final Nibbāna, simultaneously with his passing, there was a great earthquake, terrifying and hair-raising, and the celestial drums resounded.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, Brahmā Sahampati spoke this verse:
"All beings in the world shall lay down their physical frame."
Where such a Teacher exists,
the peerless one in the world,
the Tathāgata who has attained power—
“The Perfectly Enlightened One has attained final Nibbāna.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, Sakka, lord of the devas, recited this verse:
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned things;”
Subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease.
Their subsiding is blissful.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, the Venerable Anuruddha spoke these verses:
“There was neither inhalation nor exhalation for that Stable One whose mind was steadfast.”
Unperturbed, having set out for peace,
the Sage passed away at that time with a mind free from dejection.
He endured that feeling;
like the extinguishing of a lamp,
there was liberation of the mind.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, immediately upon his passing, the Venerable Ānanda spoke this verse:
“Then there was that which was terrifying;
then there was that which made the hair stand on end.”
“When the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with the excellence of all modes, has attained final Nibbāna.
When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, those monks there who were not yet free from passion, some of them, raising their arms, wailed aloud;
They fell down as if struck by a blow, whirled about, and rolled to and fro, crying out: "Too soon has the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna!
Too soon has the Sugata attained final Nibbāna! Too soon has the Eye of the World vanished from sight!
But those bhikkhus who were free from lust endured it mindfully and with clear comprehension:
“Conditioned phenomena are impermanent; how could it be otherwise?
Then the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the monks:
“Enough, friends; do not grieve, do not lament.”
"Surely, friend, this was already declared by the Blessed One:
'There is separation, dissociation, and change from all that is dear and beloved.
How, friend, could it be otherwise? It is impossible for that which is born, come to be, conditioned, and subject to disintegration not to disintegrate."
“Friends, the deities are lamenting.
“But in what manner, venerable sir, does the Venerable Anuruddha attend to the deities?
“There are, friend Ānanda, deities who perceive earth in the sky; they wail with disheveled hair, they wail with arms outstretched, they fall prostrate, they roll back and forth, crying:”
“Too soon has the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna; too soon has the Sugata attained final Nibbāna; too soon has the Eye of the World disappeared.

“Indeed, friend Ānanda, there are deities on earth who perceive earth as earth, who, tearing their hair, weep; raising their arms, they weep; falling down as if cut down, they roll back and forth, crying:
‘Too soon has the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna; too soon has the Sugata attained final Nibbāna; too soon has the Eye of the World disappeared.’”
"But those deities who are free from lust endure it mindfully and clearly comprehending:
‘Conditioned phenomena are impermanent; how could this be otherwise?
Then the Venerable Anuruddha and the Venerable Ānanda spent the remainder of that night in conversation on the Dhamma.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, friend Ānanda, enter Kusinārā and announce to the Mallas of Kusinārā:
'Vāseṭṭhas, the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna.'"
"Now, Venerable Sir, do as you deem it timely.
"Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Venerable Anuruddha. Having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, he entered Kusinārā accompanied by a single companion.
Now at that time, the Mallas of Kusinārā were assembled in the council hall for a certain business.
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the assembly hall of the Mallas of Kusinārā; having arrived, he announced to the Mallas of Kusinārā:
"Vāseṭṭhas, the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna;
do now as you deem fit."

Having heard these words of the Venerable Ānanda, the Mallas, the sons of the Mallas, the daughters-in-law of the Mallas, and the wives of the Mallas were distressed, sorrowful, and overwhelmed by mental anguish;
some, tearing at their hair, wailed; raising their arms, they wailed;
they fell down as if struck, and they writhed and rolled about, crying:
“Too soon has the Blessed One attained final nibbāna; too soon has the Sugata attained final nibbāna; too soon has the Eye of the World disappeared.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā gave orders to their men: “Prepare the funeral pyre for the Tathāgata’s body.”
“In that case, my good man, assemble all the perfumes, garlands,
and musicians from Kusinārā. Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, taking perfumes, garlands, all the musicians, and five hundred pairs of garments,
went to the Upavattana sal forest of the Mallas, where the body of the Blessed One was.
Having approached, they spent one day honoring, revering, respecting, and worshipping the body of the Blessed One with dances, songs, music, garlands, and perfumes;
they fashioned canopies of cloth and prepared circular pavilions.
Then it occurred to the Mallas of Kusinārā:
“It is indeed too late today to cremate the Blessed One’s body; we shall cremate the Blessed One’s body tomorrow.

Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, honoring, revering, esteeming, and worshipping the Blessed One’s body with dance, song, music, garlands, and perfumes, prepared canopies of cloth and prepared the circular pavilion.
They spent a second day, they spent a third day, they spent a fourth day,
they spent a fifth day, and they spent a sixth day.
Then, on the seventh day, it occurred to the Mallas of Kusinārā:
“Honoring, revering, esteeming, and worshipping the Blessed One’s body with dances, songs, music, garlands, and perfumes,
we shall carry it from the south to the south of the city, and outside the city, to the south of the city,
we shall cremate the Blessed One’s body.”
Now at that time, eight leading Mallas, having washed their heads and dressed in new clothes,
thinking, "We shall lift up the Blessed One’s body," were unable to lift it.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:

“Venerable Anuruddha, what is the cause, what is the reason, that these eight leading Mallas, having bathed their heads and dressed in unwashed robes, are unable to lift up the Blessed One’s body, saying: ‘We shall carry the Blessed One’s body’?
“Vāseṭṭhas, your intention is one thing, but the intention of the deities is another.”
“But what, venerable sir, was the intention of the deities?
“Vāseṭṭhas, your intention was this:
‘We shall honor and revere the body of the Blessed One with dance, song, music, garlands, and perfumes.’”
‘Honoring, respecting, and revering it, let us carry the Blessed One’s body from the south to the south, and from the outside to the outside, and cremate it to the south of the city’—
this, Vāseṭṭhas, was the intention of the deities.
“Honoring, respecting, cherishing, and worshipping the Blessed One’s body with divine dances, songs, music, garlands, and perfumes,
we shall carry it further and further north through the city, enter the city by the northern gate,
carry it through the center of the city, and exit by the eastern gate.”
“Let us cremate the Blessed One’s body here at the Mallas’ shrine called Makutabandhana, to the east of the city.
“Venerable sir, let it be as the devas intend.
At that time, Kusinārā was strewn knee-deep with *mandārava* flowers all the way to its moats, sewers, and narrow passages.
Then the deities and the Mallas of Kusinārā, honoring, revering, esteeming, and worshipping the Blessed One’s body with divine and human dances,
songs, music, garlands, and perfumes, carried it further and further north through the city,
entered the city by the northern gate, and proceeded through the center of the city.
Having carried [the body] through the city and having departed by the eastern gate,
they deposited the Blessed One’s body there at the Mallas’ shrine named Makuta-bandhana to the east of the city.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Venerable Ānanda, how should we proceed with the Tathāgata’s body?
“Vāseṭṭhas, one should proceed with the Tathāgata’s body in the same way as they proceed with the body of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti).
“But venerable Ānanda, how do they proceed with the body of a wheel-turning monarch?”

“Vāseṭṭhas, the body of a wheel-turning monarch is wrapped in new cloth; having wrapped it in new cloth, it is wrapped in carded cotton wool; having wrapped it in carded cotton wool, it is wrapped in new cloth.
By this method, having wrapped the body of the wheel-turning monarch in five hundred pairs [of cloth], it is placed in an iron oil-vat, which is covered with another iron vessel.
Then, having prepared a funeral pyre of all kinds of fragrant woods for the king...”
They cremate the body of the wheel-turning monarch.
At the crossroads of the four great highways, they erect a stupa for the wheel-turning monarch.
Such, Vāseṭṭhas, is the way they treat the body of a wheel-turning monarch.
“Vāseṭṭhas, just as they proceed with the body of a wheel-turning monarch, so should they proceed with the body of the Tathāgata.
A stupa for the Tathāgata should be built at the crossroads of the four great highways.
There, whatever people shall offer garlands, perfumes, or powders, or shall pay homage, or shall clear their minds, that will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.”
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā gave orders to their men:
"In that case, sirs, gather together the Mallans' carded cotton wool.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, having wrapped the Blessed One’s body in a new cloth, wrapped it in carded cotton wool; and having wrapped it in carded cotton wool, they wrapped it in a new cloth.
By this means, having wrapped the Blessed One’s body with five hundred double-folded cloths, they placed it in an iron oil-vat, which was then covered with another iron vat.
Having prepared a pyre of all kinds of fragrant scents, they placed the Blessed One’s body upon the pyre.
38. The Story of the Elder Mahākassapa.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa was traveling on the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa, having stepped down from the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Now at that time, a certain Ājīvaka was traveling on the highway from Kusinārā to Pāvā, carrying a mandārava flower from Kusinārā.
The Venerable Mahākassapa saw that Ājīvaka coming from afar; having seen him, he said this to the Ājīvaka:
"Friend, do you know our Teacher?
"Yes, friend, I know him; the ascetic Gotama attained final Nibbāna seven days ago."
"Therefore, I took this mandārava flower.
Thereupon, those monks who were not yet free from passion—some of them threw up their arms and wept; they fell down as if struck, rolling back and forth, crying out:
"Too soon has the Blessed One attained final nibbāna! Too soon has the Sugata attained final nibbāna! Too soon has the Eye of the World vanished!"
But those bhikkhus who were free from lust endured it mindfully and clearly comprehending, saying:
"Conditioned phenomena are impermanent; how could this be otherwise?
Now at that time, a man named Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, was sitting in that assembly.
Then Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, said this to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, friends, do not grieve; do not lament. We are well rid of that Great Ascetic.
We were troubled by him [thinking]: ‘This is allowable for you; this is not allowable for you.’”
“But now we shall do whatever we wish, and we shall not do what we do not wish.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
“Enough, friends; do not grieve, do not lament.”
"Indeed, friend, this was already declared by the Blessed One:
'There is separation, there is parting, there is change for all things dear and beloved.

How, friend, could it be possible here that what is born, come to being, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate—even the body of the Tathāgata? Such a thing is impossible."
Now at that time, four leading Mallas, having washed their heads and dressed in new clothes,
thinking, "We shall set fire to the Blessed One’s funeral pyre," were unable to set it alight.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:

“Venerable Anuruddha, what is the cause, what is the reason, why these four leading Mallas, having bathed their heads and put on new clothes, are unable to set fire to the Blessed One’s funeral pyre, thinking:
‘We shall set the Blessed One’s funeral pyre alight’?
“Vāseṭṭhas, it is because the intention of the deities is otherwise.”
“But what, venerable sir, was the intention of the deities?
“The intention of the deities, Vāseṭṭhas, was this:
‘This venerable Mahākassapa is traveling on the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred bhikkhus.’”
“The funeral pyre of the Blessed One will not ignite until the Venerable Mahākassapa has paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head.
“Venerable sir, let it be as the deities intend.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa went to Kusinārā, to the Makuṭabandhana shrine of the Mallas.

He approached the place where the Blessed One’s funeral pyre was located; having approached, he arranged his robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms in reverence, circumambulated the pyre three times keeping it to his right, and paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet with his head.

Those five hundred bhikkhus also arranged their robes over one shoulder, extended their joined palms in reverence, circumambulated the pyre three times keeping it to their right, and paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet with their heads.
When the Venerable Mahākassapa and those five hundred bhikkhus had paid homage, the funeral pyre of the Blessed One ignited of its own accord.
As the body of the Blessed One was burning, whatever there was of skin, or hide, or flesh, or sinews, or lymph—of these, neither ash nor soot was perceived;
only the bodily relics remained.
Just as when ghee or oil is burned, neither ash nor soot is perceived, even so,
when the Blessed One’s body was burned, whatever there was of skin, hide, flesh, sinews, or marrow, neither ash nor soot was perceived from it;
only the relics remained.
Of those five hundred pairs of garments, only two did not burn: the one that was most innermost and the one that was outermost.
When the Blessed One’s body had been consumed by fire, a stream of water appeared from the sky and extinguished the Blessed One’s funeral pyre;
water also welled up from the roots of the sal trees and extinguished the Blessed One’s funeral pyre.
The Mallas of Kusinārā also extinguished the Blessed One’s funeral pyre with all kinds of perfumed water.
Then the Mallas of Kusinārā, having erected a lattice-work of spears and surrounded it with a fence of bows for seven days in the assembly hall,
honored, revered, and paid homage to the relics of the Blessed One with dance, song, music, garlands, and perfumes.
They honored, revered, and worshipped [them].
39. The Division of the Relics:
King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha heard:
“The Blessed One has indeed attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya, and I too am a kshatriya; I too am worthy of a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and I too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.”
The Licchavis of Vesālī heard:
"The Blessed One has, it is said, attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Then the Licchavis of Vesālī dispatched a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya, and we too are kshatriyas; we too are worthy of a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and we too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.
The Sakyans residing in Kapilavatthu heard:
“The Blessed One, it is said, has attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.”
Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
"The Blessed One was the foremost of our kinsmen; we too deserve a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and we too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.
The Bulayas of Allakappa heard of this.
“The Blessed One has indeed attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Then the Bulayas of Allakappa sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya and we too are kshatriyas; we too deserve a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and we too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.”
The Koliyans of Rāmagāma heard:
"The Blessed One has, it is said, attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Then the Koliyans of Rāmagāma sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya, and we too are kshatriyas; we too are worthy of a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and we too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.
Then the brahmin of Veṭhadīpa heard:
“The Blessed One, it is said, has attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.”
Then the brahmin of Veṭhadīpa sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya and I am a brahmin; I too am worthy of a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and I too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.
The Mallas of Pāvā heard this.
“The Blessed One has indeed attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Then the Mallas of Pāvā sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā, saying:
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya, and we too are kshatriyas; we too deserve a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and we too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.”
When this was said, the Mallas of Kusinārā said to those groups and assemblies:
"The Blessed One has attained final nibbāna within our own village territory; we will not give away any portion of the Blessed One’s relics.
When this was said, the brahmin Doṇa said to those groups and assemblies:
“Listen, sirs, to my single word:
our Buddha was a teacher of patience.
It is not right that anyone should do harm to the Supreme Person.”
There might be a conflict over the portion of the body. Therefore,
all of you, sirs, being united, harmonious,
and in mutual agreement, let us divide the eight portions.
“May the stupas spread throughout the quarters,
and may many people be filled with faith toward the One with Vision.
“In that case, brahmin, you yourself should divide the relics of the Blessed One into eight equal portions.”
“Yes, sir,” Doṇa the brahmin replied to those assemblies and groups. Having divided the Blessed One’s relics into eight equal and well-portioned shares, he said to those assemblies and groups:
“Sirs, give me this urn; I too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the urn.
And they gave the urn to Doṇa the brahmin.
The Mallas of Pippalivana heard:
"It is said that the Blessed One has attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā.
Then the Mallas of Pippalivana sent a messenger to the Mallas of Kusinārā.
“The Blessed One was a kshatriya and we too are kshatriyas; we too deserve a share of the Blessed One’s relics, and we too shall erect a stupa and hold a festival for the Blessed One’s relics.
“There is no share of the Blessed One’s relics; the Blessed One’s relics have already been distributed.
Take embers from here.”
They then took away the embers.
40. The Honoring of the Relic Stupa:
Then King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha erected both a stupa and a great festival for the relics of the Blessed One at Rājagaha.
The Licchavis of Vesālī also erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One and held a great festival in Vesālī.
The Sakyans residing in Kapilavatthu also erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One and held a great festival in Kapilavatthu.
The Bulayas of Allakappa also erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One and held a great festival in Allakappa.
The Koḷiyans of Rāmagāma also erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One and held a festival in Rāmagāma.
The brahmin of Veṭhadīpa also erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One and held a festival in Veṭhadīpa.
The Mallas of Pāvā also erected a stupa for the relics of the Blessed One and held a festival in Pāvā.
The Mallas of Kusinārā also erected a stupa and held a great festival for the relics of the Blessed One at Kusinārā.
The brahmin Doṇa also erected a stupa and held a great festival for the water-pot.
The Moriyas of Pipphalivana also erected a stupa and held a great festival for the embers in the Pipphalivana forest.
Thus there were eight relic-stupas, the ninth was the urn-stupa, and the tenth was the charcoal-stupa.
Such was what occurred in the past.
Eight measures were the relics of the Visionary One.
In Jambudīpa they honor seven measures;
but in Rāmagāma, the Nāga kings honor one measure for the Supreme among Men.
One tusk was worshipped by the gods of the triple heaven,
while another is honored in the city of Gandhāra;
yet another is in the kingdom of the King of Kāliṅga.
But one [is] honored by the king of the nāgas.
By his very power, this earth is adorned with the most excellent sacrificial monuments.
Thus was this body of the One with Vision,
so well-honored by those honored by the honored,
worshipped by the lords of gods, the lords of nāgas, and the lords of men.
He was likewise honored by the best of lords of men;
having obtained this opportunity, worship him with palms joined,
for a Buddha is indeed difficult to encounter even in hundreds of aeons.
The forty even teeth,
the hair of the head, and the body hair—
all these the gods took away one by one.
The succession of world-systems.
The third [section], the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, is finished.
